\section[casarse]{casarse — to get married}

\label{lesson:ES-C488-casarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to relax, then the Spanish for to have fun.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: casarse}
\textbf{casarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to get married\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se casan en junio.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{They are getting married in June.}
\end{quote}

It goes with \emph{con}: \emph{casarse con alguien}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{casarse} is the reflexive of \emph{casar}, \textquotedblleft{}to marry\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1), built on \emph{casa}, \textquotedblleft{}house\textquotedblright{}: to marry was to set up house. \emph{Casa} is Latin \emph{casa}, \textquotedblleft{}a hut, a cottage\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{casarse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{casarse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to relax, then the Spanish for to have fun, then say \emph{casarse} again
\end{itemize}

\section[divorciarse]{divorciarse — to get divorced}

\label{lesson:ES-C488-divorciarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to have fun, then the Spanish for to get married.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: divorciarse}
\textbf{divorciarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to get divorced\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mis tíos se divorciaron hace años.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My aunt and uncle got divorced years ago.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{divorciarse} is built on \emph{divorcio}, \textquotedblleft{}divorce\textquotedblright{}, Latin \emph{divortium}, \textquotedblleft{}a separation\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{divertere}, \textquotedblleft{}to turn different ways\textquotedblright{} — the verb behind \emph{divertirse}, \textquotedblleft{}to have fun\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Divorcio} is learned: its \emph{-ti-} became \emph{-ci-}, not the \emph{z} of speech.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to have fun, then the Spanish for to get married, then say \emph{divorciarse} again

\section[enamorarse]{enamorarse — to fall in love}

\label{lesson:ES-C488-enamorarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to get married, then the Spanish for to get divorced.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: enamorarse}
\textbf{enamorarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to fall in love\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se enamoró de su vecino.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She fell in love with her neighbour.}
\end{quote}

It goes with \emph{de}: \emph{enamorarse de alguien}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{enamorarse} is \emph{en-}, \emph{amor}, \textquotedblleft{}love\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{-ar}: to go into love. \emph{Amor} is Latin \emph{amor}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[despedirse]{despedirse — to say goodbye}

\label{lesson:ES-C488-despedirse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to get divorced, then the Spanish for to fall in love.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: despedirse}
\textbf{despedirse} — \textquotedblleft{}to say goodbye\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Me despido de todos antes de salir.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I say goodbye to everyone before leaving.}
\end{quote}

The e breaks into i: \emph{me despido}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{despedirse} contains \emph{pedir}, \textquotedblleft{}to ask\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{petere}; EtymDB 2.1 traces it to \emph{de} and Latin \emph{expetere}, \textquotedblleft{}to ask for, to demand\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[saludar]{saludar — to greet, to say hello}

\label{lesson:ES-C488-saludar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to fall in love, then the Spanish for to say goodbye.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: saludar}
\textbf{saludar} — \textquotedblleft{}to greet, to say hello\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Saluda a tu madre de mi parte.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Say hello to your mother from me.}
\end{quote}

The verb behind \emph{el saludo}, the greeting.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{saludar} $\leftarrow$ Latin \emph{salutare}, \textquotedblleft{}to greet, to wish good health\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1), from \emph{salus}, \emph{salutis}, \textquotedblleft{}health\textquotedblright{} — inherited: the \emph{-t-} became \emph{-d-}. The \emph{salud} you raise a glass to is the same word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}
